content.body: Have you ever needed to shift items in a list to make room for something new? That's exactly what rotating an array does. In this lesson, you'll learn how to efficiently rotate an array using a clever lookup technique.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Explain why a brute force rotation approach is inefficient.
2. Implement an array rotation using a hash map to track element positions.
3. Determine when to check the lookup structure versus add to it during rotation.
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: Rotate the array [1, 2, 3] right by 1 position. What's the result?

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: Now rotate [5, 6, 7, 8, 9] right by 2 positions. What do you get?
content.successMessage: Excellent! Rotating right by 2 gives us [8, 9, 5, 6, 7].

content.title: One more
content.successMessage: Great work! You manually shifted elements to get [40, 50, 60, 10, 20, 30].

content.body: What you just did was a manual rotation - you visually tracked where each element should move. For small arrays this works, but for larger arrays we need a systematic approach.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When arrays have thousands of elements, manually tracking positions becomes impossible. We need a method that works for any size. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The core idea is to remember what we've already seen. Instead of manually shifting each element, we can use a lookup structure (like an object or Map) to track where each element should end up after rotation.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step. For rotation, we write down where each element's new position will be.

content.body: We'll calculate each element's new position using modular arithmetic and store it in a lookup structure.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
For array [1,2,3,4,5] rotated right by 2:
1. New position for index 0: (0+2)%5 = 2 → store 1 at position 2
2. New position for index 1: (1+2)%5 = 3 → store 2 at position 3
3. New position for index 2: (2+2)%5 = 4 → store 3 at position 4
4. New position for index 3: (3+2)%5 = 0 → store 4 at position 0
5. New position for index 4: (4+2)%5 = 1 → store 5 at position 1
Result: [4,5,1,2,3]

content.body:
1. Create an empty array for the result
2. For each element in the original array:
   a. Calculate its new position: (current index + rotation) % array length
   b. Place the element at that new position in the result array
3. Return the rotated array

content.body: Great job! You've learned how to rotate an array efficiently using position calculation. Remember: the key insight was calculating new positions with (i + k) % length and storing elements directly in their final spots. This approach avoids unnecessary shifting and works for arrays of any size.
